title: Understanding Form Templates in SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2
author: pvsbprasad
text:
Understanding Output Management in SAP Sales and Service Cloud: Main Templates, Form Templates and Rules 
 Introduction 
 Document output is an important part of many business processes in SAP Sales and Service Cloud . Business documents such as invoices, sales documents, service documents, and other forms may need to be generated as PDFs, printed, emailed, or sent to business partners. 
 SAP provides Output Management capabilities to control how these documents are generated and formatted. 
 In this blog, we will look at the key concepts involved in Output Management: 
 Form Main Templates 
 Form Templates 
 Language Variants 
 Form Template Rules 
 Adobe LiveCycle Designer 

 How the system determines which template to use 
 Understanding the relationship between these components is important when implementing customer-specific document layouts. 
 1. What is Output Management? 
 Output Management comprises the activities required to generate and distribute business documents. 
 Form-based documents can be generated: 
 On an ad hoc basis 
 As part of a business process 
 As PDF documents 
 As email attachments 
 For printing 
 For faxing, where supported 
 The overall output process can be understood using three important components: 
 Main Template → Form Template → Form Template Rule 
 The Main Template provides common branding and organizational information. 
 The Form Template defines the actual document structure and content. 
 The Form Template Rule determines which form template should be used for a particular business document and under which conditions . 

 2. Form Main Templates 
 A Form Main Template is used to define common elements that can be reused across multiple form templates. 
 For example, a company may want the same: 
 Company logo 
 Header 
 Sender address 
 Footer 
 Language-dependent footer 
 across Quotes , opp, and other business forms. 
 Instead of maintaining these elements separately in every form, you can maintain them centrally in a Main Template. 

 3. How Does the System Determine the Main Template? 
 When a business document is generated, the system follows a hierarchy to determine which Main Template should be used. 
 The basic logic is: 
 Business Document → Company/Org Unit → Parent Org Unit → Default Main Template 
 Step 1: Check the assigned organizational unit 
 The system first checks whether a Main Template is assigned to the company or organizational unit where the business document was created. 
 The system first searches for a Main Template assigned to Sales US West Coast . 
 Step 2: Search higher in the organizational structure 
 If no matching Main Template is found, the system searches upward through the organizational hierarchy. 
 Step 3: Use the default Main Template 
 If no matching Main Template is found anywhere in the organizational hierarchy, the system uses the default Main Template . 
 This allows organizations to have both global and company-specific branding. 

 4. Creating a Main Template 
 To create a Main Template, navigate to: 
 User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Output Management → Maintain Main Template 
 Choose Create . 
 Enter: 

 Main Template Name 

 Organizational Unit, if applicable 
 You can also enable the Is Default option if the template should be used as the default. 

 Designing the Main Template 
 The Main Template provides options for defining the common header and footer information. 
 Header 
 You can: 
 Upload a company logo 
 Adjust logo size and alignment 
 Enable a header divider 
 Maintain the sender address 
 Supported logo formats include: 
 .gif 
 .bmp 
 .jpg 
 .png 
 .tif 
 The logo should be within the supported size limits. If the uploaded graphic exceeds the supported dimensions, the system automatically resizes it. 
 Footer 
 You can configure the number of footer columns and maintain footer information. 
 Up to four footer blocks can be maintained, with a maximum of 10 lines per footer . 
 The footer blocks are divided equally across the available space. 

 5. Form Templates 
 While the Main Template provides common branding elements, the Form Template defines the actual layout and content of a business document. 
 Form templates are used to generate print forms, which are generally produced as PDF documents. 
 These forms can then be: 
 Printed 
 Sent as email attachments 
 Sent to business partners 
 Used as part of business processes 
 The Main Template can then provide the common company logo, sender address, and footer. 
 6. SAP-Delivered vs Custom Form Templates 
 SAP provides predefined form templates for many business scenarios. 
 Although you can create new templates, SAP recommends using and adapting the templates provided by SAP or partners where possible. 
 A typical approach is: 
 SAP-Delivered Template → Copy Template → Customize → Publish → Use in Output Rules 
 This approach has an important advantage: existing output settings can be reused instead of configuring everything from scratch. 

 7. Why Should You Copy the SAP Template? 
 Suppose SAP provides a standard Customer Invoice template. 
 Instead of creating a completely new form, you can: 
 Select the SAP-delivered template. 
 Choose Copy Template . 
 Enter a custom name and description. 
 Select the required language. 
 Enable the Form Main Template option if required. 
 Save and publish the template. 
 Your organization can then customize the copied template without directly modifying the SAP-delivered version. 
 This is particularly useful when SAP delivers a newer version of the standard template. 
 8. Editing Form Templates with Adobe LiveCycle Designer 
 For more advanced layout changes, SAP supports downloading the form template and modifying it using Adobe LiveCycle Designer . 
 The required environment includes Adobe LiveCycle Designer along with the relevant SAP support components. 
 Navigate to: 
 User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Output Management → Maintain Form Template 
 Select the required template and choose Edit . 
 Depending on the scenario, you can download the template and modify the .xdp file using Adobe LiveCycle Designer. 

 9. What Can Be Changed in Adobe LiveCycle Designer? 
 Using Adobe LiveCycle Designer, you can make several layout and formatting changes. 
 For example: 
 Layout 
 You can: 
 Change the position of fields 
 Change the position of the title 
 Change the position of the logo 
 Change field alignment 
 Change the sequence of fields 
 Formatting 
 You can: 
 Change fonts 
 Change font sizes 
 Change line styles 
 Add borders 
 Change alignment 
 Fields and Columns 
 You can: 
 Show or hide fields 
 Change field labels 
 Change column order 
 Change column headers 
 Show or hide columns 
 However, if a required field is not available in the form data structure, additional extensibility or SAP support may be required. 
 10. Language Variants 
 A business may operate across multiple countries and languages. 
 For example: 
 English 
 German 
 French 
 Spanish 
 SAP supports language variants of form templates. 
 A language variant is essentially a version of an existing form template maintained for another language. 
 To create one: 
 User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Output Management → Maintain Form Template 
 Select the required template and choose: 
 Copy Variant 
 Then select the required language. 
 11. Downloading Form Template Variants 
 A form template variant can also be downloaded for offline editing or testing. 
 Navigate to: 
 User Menu → Settings → All Settings → Output Management → Maintain Form Template 
 Select the required template and choose Download . 
 The downloaded ZIP package can contain: 
 XDP file 
 XSD file 
 Sample XML data, if available 
 The XDP contains the form template definition. 
 The XSD describes the XML data structure and is useful when editing the form offline. 
 Sample XML data can be used to preview the output. 
 If sample data is not available, XML data can also be obtained from the document's output history where supported. 
 12. Form Template Rules 
 Now we come to one of the most important parts of Output Management: 
 Form Template Rules 
 Imagine you have two invoice templates: 
 Template A 

 Domestic Quote 
 Template B 

 International Quote 
 How does the system know which template to use? 
 This is where a Form Template Rule is required. 
 A Form Template Rule defines the conditions under which a particular form template should be selected. 

 13. Main Template + Form Template + Rule: Putting Everything Together 
 The complete flow can be visualized as: 
 Business Transaction 
 ↓ 
 Output Management 
 ↓ 
 Form Template Rule 
 ↓ 
 Select Form Template 
 ↓ 
 Apply Main Template 
 ↓ 
 Generate PDF 
 ↓ 
 Print / Email / Other Output Channel 
 14. Key Takeaways 
 Here are the key concepts to remember: 
 1. Main Template 
 Used for common branding such as: 
 Logo + Header + Sender Address + Footer 
 2. Form Template 
 Defines the actual business document layout and content. 
 3. Language Variant 
 Provides the same form in another language. 
 4. Form Template Rule 
 Determines which form template should be selected based on defined conditions. 
 5. Rule Sequence 
 Specific rules should generally be evaluated before generic rules. 
 6. SAP-Delivered Templates 
 Where possible, copy and adapt SAP-delivered templates rather than creating everything from scratch. 
 7. Adobe LiveCycle Designer 
 Can be used for advanced layout and form customization where supported. 

 Conclusion 
 SAP Output Management provides a structured way to manage business document output without having to maintain every document independently. 
 The most important relationship to understand is: 
 Main Template → Common Branding 
 Form Template → Document Layout and Content 
 Form Template Rule → Template Selection Logic 
 Once these three concepts are understood, scenarios such as country-specific invoices, company-specific branding, multilingual forms, and different document layouts become easier to configure and manage. 
 For administrators and implementation teams, paying particular attention to template inheritance, language variants, rule conditions, and rule sequence can help avoid unexpected document output and simplify long-term form maintenance.

title: From AI-Ready Data to Agent-Ready Data
author: MostafaElbarbary
text:
For years, many data architecture conversations started with the same question: How do we bring data together so the business can report on it? 
 With AI agents, I think we need to add another question: 
 What does an agent need to understand before we allow it to recommend — or take — an action? 
 A dashboard may tell us that overdue receivables have increased. An agent could go much further. It might be asked to identify the customers behind the increase, check disputed invoices, recommend the next step, and even create a follow-up task. 
 That is a very different demand on the data foundation. Every one of those steps requires more than a clean table. 
 What changes for the data foundation? 
 An agent needs to understand the agreed meaning of a measure such as DSO. It needs to know the relationships between customers, invoices, and disputes. It needs to understand where each figure came from, how fresh it is, and which permissions apply to both the user and the agent. 
 Just as importantly, there needs to be a clear boundary between explaining a situation and changing it . 
 An AI response can sound completely convincing even when one of these foundations is missing. 
 Gartner describes the move toward agent-ready data in terms of whether data is suitable for agentic use and whether the agent is using it in a valid way. McKinsey also emphasizes semantics, reusable data products, relationships, governance, and observability. 
 I find both perspectives useful because they move the discussion away from a broad statement such as “our data is clean” and toward something much more specific: 
 Is this data ready for this agent, this user, this decision, and this action? 
 How I would approach this in an SAP landscape 
 SAP Business Data Cloud and its data products can provide a governed starting point. 
 SAP Datasphere can help model business meaning and make data easier to discover and consume. 
 SAP Knowledge Graph also appears in SAP’s longer-term architecture vision as a semantic grounding layer for agents. I would treat that as architectural direction rather than assuming that every capability is already available in every customer landscape today. 
 If I were starting a customer workshop, I would begin with five questions: 
 What decision should the agent support? 
 Which facts would an experienced employee check before making that decision? 
 Who owns the definitions and quality checks behind those facts? 
 What is the agent allowed to see and do? 
 How will we trace its answer back to the supporting evidence? 
 The answers to those questions tell us what data products, semantics, documents, and controls are actually required. 
 For a first release, I would often start with an agent that explains a situation and cites the supporting records. 
 If users can validate the answer consistently, we can then assess whether a controlled action makes sense. 
 This is where I see the role of the data architect evolving. Our job is no longer only to deliver the right number. We also need to establish its meaning, reliability, context, and permitted use inside a business process. 
 A practical way to make this real is to start small: one question, one user role, and one proposed action. 
 That makes the architecture testable. 
 If the answer changes when the role or proposed action changes, the underlying data product may still be valuable, but the agent design probably needs a more precise boundary. 
 This also gives the architect an important role in adoption conversations. 
 We can bring finance, process, security, and data teams around one concrete scenario and make their assumptions visible. If they disagree, that disagreement is useful evidence. It tells us where the design is still unclear. 
 It is much cheaper to resolve those questions in a workshop than after an automated action has already been taken. 

 What to read next 

 Topic 
 Why read it 
 Link to read 

 Agent readiness 
 Understand why suitability and valid data use matter for agents. 
 Open resource 

 Architecture foundations 
 Connect semantics, data products, permissions, governance, and observability. 
 Open resource 

 Business context for agents 
 Explore how SAP positions data products and semantic grounding for AI agents. 
 Open resource

title: MCP Server with Integration Suite via API Centric Integration, S/4HANA API
author: ChingHong
text:
Introduction/Scenario This post continues from the previous article, MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose S/4HANA ... - SAP Community , and focuses on addressing the identified issues by using API Artifacts. 
 Background: 
 The previous post demonstrated how to set up an MCP server with SAP Integration Suite and connect it to S/4HANA Public Cloud using OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion. This approach helps maintain governance by ensuring that S/4HANA APIs are consumed using a named user account, where access is restricted based on the authorizations and roles assigned to that user. 
 When the MCP server is used for read-only scenarios, such as HTTP GET operations, it works well with clients such as GitHub Copilot and Claude. However, several issues were encountered when attempting to perform write operations against S/4HANA Public Cloud APIs, such as HTTP POST (create) and PATCH (update) requests through the MCP server. 
 Therefore, the approach described in this post is optional and only relevant if your MCP server needs to support create or update operations on S/4HANA APIs. If your use case is limited to HTTP GET requests, you can continue to follow the implementation approach described in the previous blog without the additional steps covered here. 
 Note : SAP may enhance Integration Suite in future releases to support these scenarios out of the box. As a result, the workaround described in this post may eventually become obsolete. Before implementing this approach, always refer to the latest SAP documentation available on SAP Help Portal to verify whether a native solution is available. 

 Issue Count Issue Detail 
 1 
 Data type that interpreted as object as example below, where causing issue when calling the MCP server. 
 Thanks @MioYasutake , shared the workaround to remove the "anyOf" in the OpenAPI specification with a plain type, that shall resolve this issue if direct expose the S/4HANA API via the MCP server. 
 However, the approach shared in this blog does not need touch the OpenAPI specification. 
 2 
 Getting error as it is trying to convert the content before perform API call 
 Current workaround : Remove all the SAP_Messages and SAP__Messages from the downloaded OpenAPI file and load into the integration suite MCP server again. But this is touching the OpenAPI file that downloaded from api.sap.com. Looks like there is no other option beside touching the specification file. 

 3 
 CSRF token issue when doing HTTP Post action, looks like there is no way to enhance the MCP to send access HTTP header and update the MCP server to handle this. 

 This blog is demonstrating the possible option to resolve this. 
 4 
 ETag handling when doing HTTP patch action 
 This blog is demonstrating the possible option to resolve this. 
 5 
 Other data type issues, for example "Time" don't seem working as expected in Postman, SAP return "HH:MM:SS", but "Time" data type is expecting "HH:MM:SS{Z}" instead if not mistaken. Will need to remove the "Time Format" in the API artifact or update the OpenAPI specification prior loaded into the API artifact. 
 The response in the Postman console 
 The MCP artifact/policies only allows limited API policies application (refer - Configure an MCP Server Created from an API Artifact | SAP Help Portal ), and no message transformation or additional HTTP called is allowed. Hence, this writing is demonstrating how to use the API Centric Artifact on solving some of the mentioned issued below and still supporting user principal propagation connection to the S/4HANA Public Cloud API. 
 Note: 
 As of the date of writing, the API-centric artifacts and policies in SAP Integration Suite do not support principal propagation. During Devtoberfest 2026 From APIs to Agent Tools: How MCP Gateway changes what Integration means - YouTube , SAP indicated that this capability is on the roadmap for a future release. Therefore, this blog demonstrates a possible workaround to achieve principal propagation until native support becomes available. 
 In addition, the final section of this blog shows how principal propagation can be implemented when connecting to SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud or SAP S/4HANA On-Premise via SAP Cloud Connector. 
 Flow: → Agent (Claude/Github Copilot/any AI Agent) 
 → MCP server by Integration Suite (Authenticated via IAS)
 → API Artifact by Integration Suite (Authenticated via IAS)
 → BTP Destination Service (OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion) 
 → S/4HANA Public Cloud (executed as the authenticated user) 

 Will leverage the BTP destination API to generate SAML bearer assertion token to access the S/4HANA public cloud to overcome the limitation that API artifact don't support OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion. Reference 
 Pre-requisite: 
 SAP BTP with Cloud Foundry Enabled 
 SAP Integration Suite with MCP server, Integration Cell runtime capability 
 S/4HANA Public Cloud 
 SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) 
 AI Agent able to communicate with MCP server 
 The BTP destination to S/4HANA Public Cloud already setup - refer previous blog 
 Destination Service Instance Setup 
 Goto BTP create an destination service instance 
 Service: Destination Service 
 Plan: lite 
 Create a key and copy the Client ID, Client Secret and uri for later usage 

 Create API Artifact 
 Important: Remove all the SAP_Messages and SAP__Messages from the downloaded OpenAPI file. You may use AI assistant on helping this if not familiar on changing this. 
 Create a new API Artifact - choose Integration Cell as the Runtime Profile 

 Select URL or Specification 

 Enter the information as below 
 Filename: OpenAPI specification(downloaded from api.sap.com) and remove the SAP_Messages and SAP__Messages from the file 
 URL: URL to access the S/4HANA public cloud sales order api 
 Name: your prefer name 
 ID: your prefer ID 
 Service Type: REST 
 API Base Path: your prefer path 

 Update description if required 

 The URL here will be come irrelevant to the policies as will overwrite the auto generated endpoint 

 Resources are auto generated based on the uploaded API specification 

 Policies 
 Important here: delete the auto generated target HTTP channel, recreate a new HTTP channel to target or S/4HANA Public Cloud API, as the default generated target HTTP channel not allowing the "Authorization" header passing 

 More information can refer to the blog Secure APIs: External OIDC-Based Authentication fo... - SAP Community 
 The Well-known URL: https://<ias tenant>.accounts.ondemand.com/.well-known/openid-configuration 
 Audience: Can leave empty unless restrict to certain client ID or target system only 
 ClientID Key: standard using ${authn.oidc.jwt.azp}, where you can find out this when studying the JWT via any JWT decoder, for example: SuperTokens JWT Decoder 
 User Info Key: standard using ${authn.oidc.jwt.email}, where you can find out this when studying the JWT via any JWT decoder, for example: SuperTokens JWT Decoder 

 import com.sap.it.script.v2.api.Message;
import groovy.json.JsonOutput;
import groovy.json.JsonSlurper;

def Message storeInputInformation(Message message) {

 Map<String, Object> headers = message.getHeaders();

 // Convert to JSON string
 String headersJson = JsonOutput.prettyPrint(JsonOutput.toJson(headers))
 // Store in exchange property
 message.setProperty("OriHeaders", headersJson);

 message.setProperty("OriBody", message.getBody());

 // get token
 String authHeader = message.getHeader("Authorization", String)
 String token = authHeader?.replaceFirst(/^Bearer\s+/, "")
 message.setProperty("AccessToken", token)

 // set token for destination fetch
 message.setHeader("x-user-token", token)

 return message;
} 

 Request-Reply to Destination Service 
 Address : <uri copy from the destination service instance key>/v1/destinations/<destination created in BTP>, for example: https://destination-configuration.cfapps.us10.hana.ondemand.com/destination-configuration/v1/destinations/S4_XBB_API 
 Credential Name: The credential artifact the capture the OAuth2ClientCredential setup, this token URL, client ID and password refer to the Destination Service Instance key 
 Request Headers: x-user-token 

 Extract Token return from destination, where this Token can be used to call S/4HANA 
 def Message extractTokenFromDestination(Message message) {

 // set back original headers
 String headersJson = message.getProperty("OriHeaders")
 if (headersJson) {
 def headersMap = new JsonSlurper().parseText(headersJson)
 headersMap.each { key, value ->
 if (value != null) {
 message.setHeader(key.toString(), value.toString())
 }
 }
 }

 def json = new JsonSlurper().parseText(message.getBody(String))

 def bearerToken = json.authTokens?.find { it.type == "Bearer" }?.value
 message.setHeader("Authorization", "Bearer ${bearerToken}")
 message.setProperty("SAMLBearerAssertionToken", bearerToken);

 message.setBody(message.getProperty("OriBody"));

 return message;
} 

 Router to decide fetch CSRF token 

 Content Modifier: Set CSRF Token Fetch Header 

 Request Reply - Fetch CSRF Token 
 Address : <api URL> 
 Proxy Type: Internet 
 Method: GET 
 Authentication: none (token already set in previous step, will be pass at request header) 
 Request Headers: Authorization|x-csrf-token 
 Response Headers: * 

 Extract CSRF response cookie and set cookie def Message extractCSRFToken(Message message) {

 def cookies = message.getHeader("set-cookie");
 message.setHeader("cookie", String.join("; ", cookies));

 return message;
} 

 Router - set Etag header, set to * always also force update 

 Set the original input header and body before perform the HTTP call to the actual target API URL def Message prepareInputPriorCall(Message message) {
 // keep a copy of the cookies as this is returned by the CSRF token fetch
 def cookies = message.getHeader("cookie");

 // set back original headers
 String headersJson = message.getProperty("OriHeaders")
 if (headersJson) {
 def headersMap = new JsonSlurper().parseText(headersJson)
 headersMap.each { key, value ->
 if (value != null) {
 message.setHeader(key.toString(), value.toString())
 }
 }
 }

 // pass the bearer token as authorization header
 def bearerToken = message.getProperty("SAMLBearerAssertionToken");
 message.setHeader("Authorization", "Bearer ${bearerToken}")

 message.setBody(message.getProperty("OriBody"));

 // set back the CSRF token fetch cookie
 message.setHeader("cookie", cookies);

 return message;
} 

 Actual Request-Reply to the API URL based on the input 
 Address : <api URL>${header.camelhttppath} 
 Query: ${header.camelhttpquery} 
 Proxy Type: Internet 
 Method: Dynamic 
 Expression: ${header.camelhttpmethod} 
 Send Body: checkbox ticked 
 Authentication: none (token already set in previous step, will be pass at request header) 
 Request Headers: * 
 Response Headers: * 
 Setup the MCP server in Integration Suite 
 Information: Configure an MCP Server Created from an API Artifact | SAP Help Portal 

 Create a new MCP server in Integration Suite 
 Source Type - API 

 Select the API, Enter name, ID, MCP Path, Version 

 Select the tools and click Add 

 Remain all auto generated item and deploy the MCP server 

 Include the MCP server into the Product. Refer to the previous blog on how to setup product 

 Test the new MCP server in Github Copilot 
 Note: Refer to previous blog on how to setup connection to MCP server in VS Code 
 Scenarios : 
 Get order detail 
 Create a new order 
 Update order 
 1 
 Get order detail 
 2 
 Create new order via MCP 

 The payload that used to call MCP server - there is no issue passing the quantity in integer format now. 
 3 
 Update the sales order reference 
 Sample payload call MCP server 

 Similar concepts communicate with S/4HANA Private Cloud or Onpremise via Cloud Connector (Principal Propagation) 
 Note: 
 The trial account used throughout this blog is not connected to a SAP Cloud Connector and therefore cannot access an SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud or SAP S/4HANA On-Premise system. For the demon

title: 103/105 & 107/109 Two-Step Goods Receipt in SAP EWM Using VL60
author: Asmithaa
text:
Introduction 
 Receiving materials from a vendor into inventory does not always follow a single process. Depending on the business requirement, different goods receipt processes may be used, and SAP provides various movement types to support these scenarios. The most used movement type for goods receipt is 101 , where the receipt is posted directly against the purchase order or inbound delivery. 
 SAP also provides two-step goods receipt processes , namely 103/105 and 107/109 . In a classic Inventory Management (IM) storage location, these processes can be executed using transactions such as MIGO . However, when the receiving storage location is EWM-managed , the process differs because the goods receipt needs to be integrated with Extended Warehouse Management (EWM). 
 In this blog, we will explore how the 103/105 and 107/109 two-step goods receipt processes work for EWM-managed storage locations, using transaction VL60. 
 107/109: 
 The business utilizes the 107/109 movement types when they need to record the stock as valuated blocked stock in transit to pay the vendor (107), then verify it once the stock is received in the warehouse (109). The table below helps us understand the two movement types a bit better. 

 The steps are a bit different from our normal flow as highlighted here: 
 Create Purchase Order 
 Create Inbound Delivery in VL60 (for 109 movement type) 
 Go to MIGO to post GRN for 107 movement type. 
 Process the Inbound delivery created in VL60 in EWM to post Goods Receipt. 
 Let’s look into all these steps in detail. 
 Step 1: Create Purchase Order in ME21N with the confirmation control key as 0004. 

 Step 2: Go to VL60, select Inbound delivery, and click on Create. 

 By default, SAP has already provided the Delivery type and item category mapped for movement type 109, so we will select the standard document type available in the transaction. 
 Step 3: Click on the Administration tab and select the Delivery type as ELST to receive the Valuated stock in Transit. 

 Step 4: In the Basic Data tab, enter the external identification data. Under Overview, enter the reference document as Purchase Order and the reference item number as the purchase order item number, then scroll left to enter the quantity. 

 Step 5: Check and save. The Inbound delivery is created. 

 Do not process this delivery yet. We must post the goods receipt against movement type 107 first, and then follow on by processing the delivery for movement type 109. 
 Step 6: Now go to MIGO and post the goods receipt against the purchase order for movement type 107. 

 The GRN is posted, and the accounting documents are also generated, since the stock is received as valuated blocked stock. 

 In MMBE, we can see the stock listed under Valuated Stock in Transit. 

 Step 7: Now we can take the Inbound delivery to process it in EWM to post the goods receipt. 

 After posting the goods receipt in EWM, if we go back to ME23N and check the purchase order history, we can see the record of both movement types. 

 Here the movement 109 doesn’t produce any financial documents. 

 103/105: 
 After receiving the goods, the business sometimes holds them in a location to inspect or verify them before the stock is finally accepted and placed into inventory. This is done in two steps: first, the stock is received as GR blocked stock (103); then, during final receipt, the blocked stock is moved to unrestricted (105), where the financial postings are done. The table below provides a summary of both movement types. 

 We don’t have a standard delivery type for this transaction, so let’s create a custom document type. The setup below helps us create the custom document type. 
 Step 1: First define the Delivery type. 
 Go to SPRO -> Logistics execution -> Shipping -> Deliveries -> Define Delivery types. 
 I have taken a copy of the ELST delivery type and created a custom delivery type, ZGBS. 

 Step 2: Create custom item category in VOV7 

 Step 3: Go to SPRO -> Logistics execution -> Shipping -> Deliveries -> Define Delivery item categories. 
 I have taken a copy of the ELST item category as well and created a custom item category, ZGBS. 

 Step 4: Now we map the delivery type and item category using the path below: 
 SPRO -> Logistics execution -> Shipping -> Deliveries -> Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries. 

 Step 5: Map the document type and item type from ERP to EWM so the delivery can be processed in EWM, using the paths below: 
 Document type mapping: SCM -> EWM -> Interfaces -> ERP Integration -> Delivery Processing -> Map Document Types from ERP System to EWM 

 Item type mapping : SCM -> EWM -> Interfaces -> ERP Integration -> Delivery Processing -> Map Item Types from ERP System to EWM 

 Once the above steps are configured in the system, the same flow of 107/109 can be followed here as well by selecting the custom delivery type in the VL60 transaction. 
 Conclusion: 
 This blog covered the two-step goods receipt process for EWM-managed storage locations using the VL60 transaction, other than the standard 101 movement type still handled through VL31N. The business can now receive goods through either process, depending on what best fits its operational needs.

title: Renovate or Re-Platform? A Strategic Roadmap for Modernising Custom ABAP Applications
author: IgorPrudnecionok
text:
This blog walks through the full arc — from understanding the risk of legacy custom ABAP to making the renovate-or-re-platform decision and shaping a clean core strategy. 

 Legacy Custom Code - Strategic Risk 
 Across global enterprises, decades of classic ABAP custom code have accumulated in ECC and early S/4HANA implementations. This is not just a development concern — it is a strategic liability sitting at the heart of your business operations. 
 Two patterns dominate the field today. The first is brownfield carry-over : classic ABAP developments migrated from ECC to S/4HANA “as-is”, never re-evaluated against modern extensibility options. The system runs, but the architecture has not evolved. The second is greenfield but not clean : new S/4HANA implementations built with classic ABAP because project teams were unaware of — or not yet trained on — Clean Core tools such as ABAP Cloud, Key User Extensibility, and the RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP). 
 The cost of inaction compounds over time. Blocked upgrades. Rising maintenance spend. Incompatibility with cloud innovations — including embedded AI capabilities such as SAP Joule, which requires a clean, standard-aligned core to deliver its full value. With SAP’s continuous delivery model for S/4HANA Cloud and the end of mainstream maintenance for SAP Business Suite 7 approaching in 2027 (SAP Note 1648480), technical debt in custom ABAP is no longer a background risk — it is a front-line strategic concern. 

 What "Clean Core" Actually Means for Custom Extensions 
 “Clean Core” is one of the most frequently cited — and frequently misunderstood — concepts in the SAP ecosystem. Let us clarify: Clean Core is not about zero customisation. It is about smart, upgrade-stable customisation. 
 A system has a clean core when its custom extensions are decoupled from SAP standard code and interact with SAP business objects exclusively through well-defined, released interfaces. Extensions can still be rich, sophisticated, and deeply integrated — but they must not break during upgrades, and the upgrade cycle must not be broken by them. 
 SAP formalised this principle in August 2025 with the introduction of the Clean Core Level concept, classifying extensions into four maturity levels: 
 Level A — the cleanest: built on-stack with ABAP Cloud or side-by-side on SAP BTP using SAP Build, CAP, or low-code/no-code tools. Fully upgrade-stable. 
 Level B — classic ABAP extensions using recommended classic APIs and accepted development technologies. Still considered clean core. 
 Level C — conditionally clean: extensions using internal SAP objects, acceptable only with additional governance checks (changelog for SAP objects) before upgrades. 
 Level D — not clean core: modifications, not-recommended SAP objects, implicit enhancements. These create direct upgrade risk. 
 This four-level model provides a practical maturity lens to classify the existing extension portfolio, define a clear target state, and proactively manage the risks associated with different clean core levels. The single source of truth for the classification criteria is SAP Note 3578329. 
 Key Reference: 
 • ABAP Extensibility Guide — Clean Core for SAP S/4HANA Cloud (August 2025) 

 The Strategic Decision: Renovate vs. Re-Platform 
 Here is one of the most persistent misconceptions in the field: Clean Core does not mean moving everything to SAP BTP. That oversimplification leads to poor architecture decisions, inflated costs, and unnecessary complexity. 
 The correct framing is a hybrid model — two complementary modernisation paths selected based on architectural coupling: 

 Approach 
 When to Apply 
 Target Platform 

 Renovate 
 Extension is tightly coupled to SAP standard processes, tables, or business objects 
 SAP S/4HANA core — using ABAP Cloud, Key User Extensibility, released BAdIs and APIs 

 Re-Platform 
 Extension is loosely coupled: standalone UIs, independent workflows, cross-system orchestration 
 SAP BTP — using CAP, BTP ABAP Environment, SAP Build, Event Mesh, Integration Suite 

 Hybrid 
 Most real-world scenarios 
 Combination of both platforms 
 Coupling is the decisive factor — not preference, convenience, or team familiarity. As a general principle, extensions that are tightly coupled to SAP standard business objects and data models tend to stay on the S/4HANA core, while standalone applications and cross-system integrations are natural candidates for SAP BTP. However, the right placement depends on the specific coupling characteristics of each extension — a structured assessment using AEM helps determine this for each use case. 
 Getting this distinction right at the architectural level is where the real value lies — and it is exactly what the SAP Application Extension Methodology is designed to support. 

 The SAP Application Extension Methodology (AEM): A Structured Decision Framework 
 Making the renovate-vs-re-platform decision systematic and repeatable — rather than relying on tribal knowledge or ad-hoc judgment — requires a structured methodology. That is precisely what the SAP Application Extension Methodology (AEM) provides. 
 AEM is a structured, technology-agnostic methodology for assessing extension use cases and defining a target clean solution architecture. It is available on the SAP Help Portal with downloadable templates and can be applied to individual use cases or as a broader governance framework. 
 The methodology follows three phases, each producing documented, reusable outputs: 
 Assess the Use Case — Align all stakeholders on the systems landscape, business context, and requirements before any technology decision is made. 
 Classify Extension Tasks — Break the use case into technology-agnostic tasks by extension style (presentation, application, and data tier) and map each task to its natural domain. 
 Define the Target Architecture — Map tasks to specific technologies and document the implementation roadmap. With AEM v2.4, each Technical Extension Building Block is tagged with a Clean Core Level (A–D), making the assessment directly traceable to SAP’s extensibility governance model. 
 AEM creates a shared language across business, functional, and technical stakeholders. Its templates are reusable across multiple renovation projects, forming the basis for an enterprise-wide extension governance framework.

 Key Pre-Conditions and Governance Concerns 
 Before launching a renovation initiative, four prerequisites must be in place. Treat these as gates — not optional considerations. 
 Prerequisite 1 — S/4HANA first. Renovation and re-platforming are S/4HANA concerns. Clean Core tools — ABAP Cloud, Key User Extensibility, RAP — are not available on ECC. An S/4HANA transformation project must be in place or completed before meaningful extension modernisation can begin. 
 Prerequisite 2 — Fit-to-Standard before building. Confirm the requirement is a genuine gap. Never invest in renovating a custom extension that replicates functionality already delivered by SAP standard. Every renovation candidate must pass a fit-to-standard check first. 
 Prerequisite 3 — One use case at a time. This is not a bulk “lift and shift” exercise. Each renovation effort should focus on a single, well-scoped business use case. System-wide custom code portfolio analysis is a separate — and equally important — exercise (see SAP Intelligent Custom Code Management). 
 Prerequisite 4 — Build the knowledge baseline. Teams need a working understanding of S/4HANA extensibility options and BTP capabilities before architectural decisions can be made. SAP offers dedicated enablement workshops as a recommended starting point. 
 Governance angle: 
 AEM’s templates and decision rationale documentation serve as the foundation for an extension governance framework — ensuring consistent, auditable, and repeatable decisions across all renovation projects in an enterprise program. 
 SAP Activate underpins a clean core journey by combining prescriptive methodology, standardized content, and governance-ready tooling to help customers adopt and run standard capabilities, minimize modifications, and guide compliant extensibility throughout the lifecycle. 

 The Renovation Journey: Major Steps 
 The following roadmap outlines the major milestones from initial knowledge-building to a production-ready clean architecture: 
 Build the knowledge foundation — Understand Clean Core, ABAP Cloud, Key User Extensibility, RAP, and SAP BTP extension options. SAP offers enablement workshops to align all project stakeholders on the art of the possible. 
 Analyse the custom code landscape — Use SAP Intelligent Custom Code Management (ICCM) to gain transparency over the existing portfolio and classify custom objects by business relevance, upgrade risk, and renovation potential. 
 Prioritise use cases — Select renovation candidates based on business value, upgrade risk, and architectural complexity. Use the clustering results, which is an output of ICCM, as prioritisation input. 
 Assess and design using AEM — SAP provides structured analysis and architecture design workshops using the Application Extension Methodology, delivering a validated target architecture and implementation roadmap. 
 Validate the results — Review technology recommendations, decision rationale, and the target solution architecture with all stakeholders before proceeding to implementation. 
 Build or commission the solution — Implementation of the clean target architecture, optionally supported by SAP advisory services including Proof-of-Concept (PoC) engagements for technically complex scenarios. 

 What the Target Architecture Looks Like 
 A renovated, Clean Core-compliant solution architecture typically follows a hybrid pattern: S/4HANA core and SAP BTP working in concert , with a clear separation of concerns and well-defined integration boundaries. 
 On the S/4HANA core: 
 Key User Extensibility — custom fields, custom logic, and custom business objects created through in-app tools, without writing code 
 Developer Extensibility via ABAP Cloud / RAP — upgrade-stable extensions using only released APIs, BAdIs, and extension points 
 Data model extensions through released CDS view extensions 
 On SAP BTP: 
 New SAP Fiori / SAPUI5 applications replacing legacy SAP GUI / ALV-based interfaces 
 Loosely coupled business logic built with CAP on Cloud Foundry or in the BTP ABAP Environment using RAP 
 Event-driven integrations using SAP Integration Suite and SAP (Advanced) Event Mesh 
 Process automation and low-code scenarios using SAP Build 
 What this architecture delivers: 
 Upgrade stability — extensions survive SAP release upgrades without rework 
 Independent “deployability” and scalability — BTP-based components follow their own release cycles and they use hardware resources that are scalable on-demand 
 Innovation agility — a clean foundation ready to absorb SAP’s AI innovations, including embedded Joule capabilities, agentic AI, and the rapidly expanding landscape of SAP Business AI 

 Why Act Now 
 Technical debt in custom ABAP is a compounding liability. The longer it stays unaddressed, the harder and more expensive modernisation becomes — and the wider the gap grows between your organisation and the innovation frontier. 
 Consider what is at stake: 
 AI readiness. SAP’s most advanced AI capabilities — Joule’s autonomous agents, embedded AI in S/4HANA business processes, AI-assisted development with Joule for Developers — require a clean, standard-aligned core. A “dirty” core blocks the very innovations that deliver competitive differentiation. In 2026 and beyond, clean core is not just an architectural preference — it is the prerequisite for enterprise AI adoption. 
 Continuous upgrade readiness. SAP’s delivery model for S/4HANA Cloud is built on frequent, continuous updates.
